english: have no choice but to / can't help but (it's the only option)
formNote: Built from 수 ('way, possibility') + 밖에 ('except, outside of') + 없다 ('not exist'), so it literally says 'there is no way except doing it' — i.e. that one action is the sole remaining option, and you're resigned to it. Attach -ㄹ 수밖에 없다 to vowel stems (가다 → 갈 수밖에 없다), -을 수밖에 없다 to consonant stems (먹다 → 먹을 수밖에 없다); ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ (살다 → 살 수밖에 없다). Past: -(으)ㄹ 수밖에 없었어요. CONTRAST: don't confuse it with the plain ability/possibility -(으)ㄹ 수 있다/없다. 갈 수 없어요 = 'I can't go (it's impossible)'; 갈 수밖에 없어요 = 'I have no choice but to go (going is the only option left).' The 밖에 flips the meaning from impossibility to inevitability. Note 밖에 always pairs with a negative (없다), and here it grammatically requires no 안 — 없다 already carries the negation. With adjectives it means 'is bound to be ~' (비싸다 → 비쌀 수밖에 없다 = it can't help but be expensive). PITFALL: English speakers reach for '~할 수 없다' when they mean 'I'm forced to'; that backfires into 'I cannot.' Also resist a space inside 수밖에.
usage: 기다릴 수밖에 없어요
I have no choice but to wait
Resigned to the only option; 없어요 carries the negation, no 안 needed
참을 수밖에 없었어요
I had no choice but to put up with it
Past frame: stem + -(으)ㄹ 수밖에 없었어요
비쌀 수밖에 없죠
Of course it's expensive (it can't help but be)
Adjective 비싸다 + 죠 = 'naturally, as you'd expect'
갈 수밖에 없었어
I had no choice but to go
Casual 반말; forced by circumstances, not by desire
examples: 막차 끊겨서 택시 탈 수밖에 없었어요.
The last train was gone, so I had no choice but to take a taxi.
막차 끊기다 = miss the last train; -아서 gives the cause that forced the only option
월급은 그대론데 물가는 오르니까 아낄 수밖에 없죠.
My salary's the same but prices keep rising, so of course I have to save.
-(으)니까 supplies the reason; 죠 invites agreement that this is the obvious result
사장님이 시키는데 야근할 수밖에 없잖아.
The boss tells me to, so I've got no choice but to work overtime.
-잖아 frames it as something the listener already knows; status (사장님) makes refusal impossible
mistakes: Writing a space inside the chunk (수 밖에) — 수밖에 is one unit (modifier + 수 + 밖에), then 없다 stands alone: 갈 수밖에 없어요.
Using the present modifier 가는 수밖에 — the form is the future/irrealis modifier -(으)ㄹ + 수밖에 없다 (갈 수밖에 없다), never 가는 수밖에.
Confusing it with 갈 수 없다 ('cannot go'). Adding 밖에 reverses the sense to 'have no choice but to go,' so don't treat them as the same negative.

english: there's no way that / it can't possibly be that
formNote: 리 here is the dependent noun 理 (Sino-Korean 'reason, principle'), so the phrase literally says 'there is no reason/grounds for it to be so' — a confident logical denial, not a wishy-washy guess. Attach -ㄹ 리가 없다 to vowel stems (오다 → 올 리가 없다), -을 리가 없다 to consonant stems (먹다 → 먹을 리가 없다). For a past doubt use -았/었을 리가 없다 (갔을 리가 없다 = no way they went); for nouns, N + 일 리가 없다 (사실 → 사실일 리가 없다). The 가 is routinely dropped in speech: -(으)ㄹ 리 없어요. CONTRAST: -(으)ㄹ 리가 없다 vs -(으)ㄹ 리 만무하다 — both mean 'no way,' but 만무하다 (萬無, 'utterly absent') is bookish/written (올 리 만무하다 reads like an essay), while 리가 없다 is everyday spoken. Also distinguish it from the soft hedge -(으)ㄹ지도 모르다 ('might'): 리가 없다 is the opposite pole — strong disbelief, 'surely not.' REGISTER: it carries emotional conviction (often surprise or indignation), so it lands naturally with -잖아/-는데. PITFALL: English speakers map 'there's no way' to time/possibility and grope for 방법(method) or 가능성(possibility); the idiomatic word is 리, and it must follow the -(으)ㄹ modifier, never stand alone.
usage: 그럴 리가 없어요
There's no way that's the case
Set phrase of disbelief; 그럴 = 그렇다's -(으)ㄹ form
걔가 그랬을 리가 없어
No way he did that
Past doubt → -았을 리가 없다, denying a completed action
벌써 도착했을 리 없어요
There's no way they've arrived already
가 dropped (리 없어요) — very natural in speech
이게 무료일 리가 없잖아
There's no way this is free
Noun 이다 → N + 일 리가 없다; 잖아 appeals to shared common sense
examples: 그 맛집이 오늘 한가할 리가 없어요. 웨이팅 엄청날걸요.
No way that famous spot is quiet today — the wait's probably huge.
맛집 = popular eatery; adjective 한가하다 takes 할 리가, then -(으)ㄹ걸요 adds a guess
걔가 나 좋아할 리가 없잖아. 김칫국 마시지 마.
There's no way he likes me. Don't get ahead of yourself.
김칫국 마시다 = assume too soon; 잖아 leans on what 'we both know'
월세가 이 가격일 리가 없는데, 사기 아니에요?
There's no way the rent is this cheap — isn't it a scam?
N + 일 리가 없다 for nouns; -는데 sets up the suspicious follow-up question
mistakes: Treating 리 as a free word or a verb stem — this 리 (理 'reason') is a dependent noun and must follow the modifier -(으)ㄹ; you can't say 리가 없다 on its own.
Using present 할 리가 없다 when you mean a past event. 할 리가 없다 = 'no way he would (do it)'; to deny something already done you need 했을 리가 없다.
Swapping in 가능성이 없다 ('there's no possibility') for the emotional 'no way!' — that's flatter and more clinical; native disbelief uses 리가 없다.

english: it's basically / it amounts to / you could say (when you do the math)
formNote: 셈 is a native Korean noun meaning 'a count, a reckoning' (from 세다 'to count'), so this pattern frames a situation as 'when you tally it up, it effectively equals X' — reality isn't literally X, but practically counts as X. Present verbs take -는 셈이다 (사는 → 사는 셈이다), past/completed verbs -(으)ㄴ 셈이다 (끝나다 → 끝난 셈이다), adjectives -(으)ㄴ 셈이다 (싸다 → 싼 셈이다). Often paired with 거의 ('almost') or 다 ('all'). CONTRAST: -는 셈이다 vs -(으)ㄴ/는 셈 치다 — 셈이다 states a calculated fact ('it amounts to ~'), whereas 셈 치다 means 'let's pretend/treat it as' a deliberate choice to regard something a certain way (속은 셈 치자 = 'let's just consider ourselves cheated and move on'). Also distinguish from -나 마나 (next door in this set): 셈이다 says 'it practically counts AS done,' not 'doing it is pointless.' REGISTER: neutral, very common in casual reasoning and explanations. PITFALL: English 'basically' is also a filler; here 셈이다 is a genuine equivalence claim, so don't tack it on to a literally-true statement (다 한 셈이에요 = 'practically done,' NOT '100% finished'). Match the modifier to tense — 끝난 셈 for a finished thing, not 끝나는 셈.
usage: 거의 다 한 셈이에요
It's basically all done
Completed action → -(으)ㄴ 셈이다 (한 셈); 거의 다 = 'almost entirely'
공짜로 산 셈이죠
It's basically like I got it for free
When a discount is so huge it tallies up to free
매일 야근하는 셈이에요
I'm basically working overtime every day
Ongoing/habitual → -는 셈이다 (하는 셈)
싸게 먹은 셈 쳐
Just count it as having eaten cheap
셈 치다 = deliberately 'consider it as' (a choice), vs 셈이다 = it amounts to
examples: 할인까지 하면 거의 반값에 산 셈이에요.
With the discount, I basically bought it half price.
Doing the mental math on a deal; 산 셈 (past action) + 거의 reinforcing the estimate
출퇴근에 두 시간이면 하루의 절반을 길에서 보내는 셈이죠.
Two hours commuting means you basically spend half your day on the road.
출퇴근 = commute; 보내는 셈 (ongoing) + 죠 invites the listener to agree with the tally
이번 달 회식이 다섯 번이면 거의 매주 모인 셈이네.
Five company dinners this month means we basically met every week.
회식 = team dinner; 모인 셈 (completed); -네 marks a fresh realization while doing the math
mistakes: Mismatching the modifier: a finished thing is 끝난 셈, an ongoing one is 하는 셈, an adjective is 싼 셈 — don't say 끝나는 셈 for something already over.
Treating it as a literal '100%' claim. 다 한 셈이에요 means 'practically done,' so don't use it when the task is truly, fully complete.
Confusing 셈이다 (it amounts to) with 셈 치다 (let's pretend it is). 없던 일로 한 셈 치자 = 'let's just treat it as if it never happened' — a chosen stance, not a calculated fact.

english: might / may / it's possible that (I'm not sure)
formNote: Composed of the indirect-question modifier -(으)ㄹ지 ('whether ~') + 도 ('even') + 모르다 ('not know'), so it literally means 'I don't even know whether it'll happen' = there's a genuine chance. Attach -ㄹ지도 모르다 to vowel stems (오다 → 올지도 모르다), -을지도 모르다 to consonant stems (늦다 → 늦을지도 모르다). Past possibility: -았/었을지도 몰라요 (갔을지도 몰라요 = might have gone). 도 can drop for a slightly firmer hunch: -(으)ㄹ지 몰라요. CONTRAST: -(으)ㄹ지도 모르다 vs -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 — both render 'might/probably,' but -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 is an impression from evidence ('looks like it will,' 비 올 것 같아요 watching dark clouds), while -(으)ㄹ지도 모르다 flags an uncertain possibility you want the listener to brace for ('it might rain, just so you know'). It also sits opposite -(으)ㄹ 리가 없다 in this set: 리가 없다 = strong denial, -(으)ㄹ지도 모르다 = open uncertainty. REGISTER: neutral; frequently used to soften warnings or hedge plans. PITFALL: 모르다 normally means 'don't know,' so beginners read 올지도 몰라요 as 'I don't know if it comes' — but as a fixed pattern it means 'might come.' Keep the -(으)ㄹ지 modifier intact; -는지/-(으)ㄴ지 would shift the time reference.
usage: 비 올지도 몰라요
It might rain
Hedged weather guess; vowel stem 오다 → 올지도
늦을지도 몰라
I might be late
Warning a friend in advance; consonant stem 늦다 → 늦을지도
벌써 갔을지도 몰라요
They might have already left
Past possibility → -았을지도 (completed action)
바쁠지도 모르니까 미리 물어봐
He might be busy, so ask ahead
Adjective 바쁘다 + -(으)니까 reason clause leading to advice
examples: 주말이라 그 카페 사람 많을지도 몰라요. 예약하고 가요.
It's the weekend so that cafe might be packed — let's reserve.
Adjective 많다 → 많을지도; the hedge motivates the practical follow-up
답장 늦을지도 몰라. 나 오늘 회의 빡세거든.
I might be slow to reply — I've got back-to-back meetings today.
빡세다 = grueling (casual); -거든 supplies the reason behind the warning
면접 결과 다음 주에 나올지도 몰라서 계속 메일 확인하고 있어요.
The interview result might come next week, so I keep checking my email.
면접 = job interview; -아서 links the possibility to the resulting behavior
mistakes: Reading 모르다 as 'don't know' here — 올지도 몰라요 is the fixed pattern 'might come,' not 'I don't know whether it comes.'
Using 올지도 몰랐어요 when you mean 'it might have come.' Past possibility lives in the verb stem (왔을지도 몰라요); 몰랐어요 only describes a past state of not knowing.
Reaching for -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 when you specifically want to warn of an unsure risk. 늦을 것 같아요 = 'I think I'll be late (impression)'; 늦을지도 몰라요 = 'I might be late (brace yourself).'

english: is bound to / naturally tends to (it's only natural that)
formNote: 마련 is a native noun meaning 'a settled arrangement / the way things are set up,' so '-기 마련이다' states that an outcome is built into the nature of things — it's bound to happen, by default. Attach -기 마련이다 straight to any verb or adjective stem with no sound change (늙다 → 늙기 마련이다, 바쁘다 → 바쁘기 마련이다, 실수하다 → 실수하기 마련이다); nouns take N(이)기 마련이다. A fully synonymous variant is -게 마련이다 (실수하게 마련이다) — same meaning, freely interchangeable. CONTRAST: -기 마련이다 vs -(으)ㄹ 수밖에 없다 — both touch 'inevitability,' but 마련이다 is a calm general truth about how the world tends to work ('people are bound to age'), while 수밖에 없다 is one person's forced choice in a specific situation ('I had no choice but to take a taxi'). REGISTER: neutral-to-reflective, the voice of proverbs and life lessons; it carries a soothing, philosophical tone, great for reassuring someone. PITFALL: English speakers borrow 'I'm bound to be late today' and try 마련이다 for a one-off — wrong; it's strictly for repeating, general truths, not a single scheduled event. Also attach to the bare stem, never the present modifier (실수하기/실수하게 마련, never 실수하는 마련).
usage: 사람은 누구나 실수하기 마련이에요
Everyone is bound to make mistakes
Comforting life truth; bare stem 실수하기 + 누구나 ('anyone')
처음엔 다 서툴기 마련이죠
Everyone's clumsy at first, naturally
Adjective 서투르다 → 서툴기; 죠 invites shared agreement
바쁘면 잊어버리기 마련이야
When you're busy you're bound to forget
Casual general truth; -면 sets the recurring condition
싼 게 비지떡이기 마련이에요
Cheap things are bound to be low quality
Proverb-style N(이)기 마련; 비지떡 = cheap, shoddy thing
examples: 혼자 살면 처음엔 외롭기 마련이에요. 곧 적응돼요.
Living alone, you're bound to feel lonely at first. You'll adjust soon.
Reassuring a newcomer; adjective 외롭다 → 외롭기; 적응되다 = get used to it
연애 초반엔 다 콩깍지가 씌기 마련이지.
In the early days of dating, everyone's bound to be lovestruck.
콩깍지(가) 씌다 = be blinded by love; -지 softens it into a shared truism
월급날 지나면 통장은 텅 비기 마련이에요.
After payday, your bank account is bound to end up empty.
통장 = bank account; -면...마련이다 states the recurring, every-month pattern
mistakes: Using it for a one-time, specific event ('오늘 늦기 마련이에요' for 'I'm bound to be late today') — it only describes general, repeating truths, not a single occasion.
Attaching the present modifier -는: it's 실수하기 마련이다 or 실수하게 마련이다, never 실수하는 마련이다.
Forgetting nouns need (이)기: 'cheap things are bound to be shoddy' is 비지떡이기 마련이다, not 비지떡 마련이다.

english: no point doing it / whether you do it or not (the result's the same)
formNote: This sets the connective -(으)나 ('whether one does') against 마나 (a contracted -(으)나 of 말다, 'to not do'), so it weighs 'doing it' against 'not doing it' and concludes the two come out identical — hence 'no point.' Attach -나 마나 to vowel/ㄹ stems (보다 → 보나 마나) and -으나 마나 to consonant stems (먹다 → 먹으나 마나); ㄹ-stems keep ㄹ (살다 → 사나 마나). It very often freezes into the adverb 보나 마나 = 'obviously, clearly (no need to even look).' CONTRAST: -(으)나 마나 vs -든지 말든지 — both involve 'do or don't,' but -(으)나 마나 means 'the outcome is the same, so it's futile' (your speaker's verdict), while -든지 말든지 means 'do it or not, I don't care / it's up to you' (indifference/leaving it to the other). Saying 가나 마나 = 'going won't change anything'; 가든지 말든지 = 'go or don't, whatever.' REGISTER: casual, slightly blunt — it dismisses the action as pointless, so use it among friends, not when politely deferring to a superior. PITFALL #1: 마나 comes from 말다, so never write 마라/말아 here. PITFALL #2: it's verb-only — you cannot say an adjective like 예쁘나 마나.
usage: 보나 마나 뻔해요
It's obvious without even looking
Frozen adverb 보나 마나 = 'clearly, predictably'; 뻔하다 = be obvious
물어보나 마나죠
There's no point even asking
The answer is a foregone conclusion; 죠 invites agreement
하나 마나 한 얘기야
That's a pointless thing to say
-나 마나 한 N = a useless/futile N (한 = modifier of 하다)
가나 마나예요
There's no point going
Going vs not going yields the same result, so it's futile
examples: 보나 마나 또 늦을 거야. 걔 원래 그래.
He'll obviously be late again. That's just how he is.
보나 마나 as the adverb 'obviously'; casual 반말 prediction
세일 가나 마나예요. 인기 사이즈는 벌써 다 품절이거든요.
No point going to the sale — the popular sizes are already sold out.
품절 = sold out; -거든요 supplies the reason it's futile
걔한테 비밀 말하나 마나야. 어차피 다 소문나거든.
There's no point telling him a secret — it'll get out anyway.
소문나다 = become a rumor; 어차피 = 'anyway, in any case' reinforces the futility
mistakes: Writing 마라/말아 instead of 마나 — the second half is the -(으)나 form of 말다, so the fixed shape is just -(으)나 마나.
Applying it to adjectives (예쁘나 마나) — it's strictly for action verbs; states/qualities can't be 'done or not done.'
Mixing it up with -든지 말든지. 가나 마나 = 'going is pointless (same result)'; 가든지 말든지 = 'go or not, I don't care.' Different intent.

english: half-heartedly / barely (do something in a half-done, distracted way)
formNote: 둥 is a dependent noun meaning roughly 'in such a manner,' and the pattern juxtaposes 'doing (-는 둥)' with 'not doing (마는 둥, from 말다),' painting an action performed so half-heartedly it's barely happening — distracted, rushed, going through the motions. Attach -는 둥 마는 둥 to a verb stem (먹다 → 먹는 둥 마는 둥, 듣다 → 듣는 둥 마는 둥); ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ (놀다 → 노는 둥 마는 둥). It's usually capped with 하다 or another verb describing what you did instead. CONTRAST: -는 둥 마는 둥 vs -(으)나 마나 — they look like cousins (both pair a verb with 말다) but mean opposite things. -는 둥 마는 둥 describes HOW you did it (sloppily, half-done — 밥을 먹는 둥 마는 둥 = 'picked at the food'); -(으)나 마나 judges that doing it is POINTLESS because the result won't change (먹으나 마나 = 'no point eating'). Don't swap them. REGISTER: casual and vivid, slightly critical — it usually conveys distraction or lack of sincerity, so it's for describing behavior you found half-baked. PITFALL: the modifier of 말다 here is 마는 (the ㄹ drops before -는), so never write 말는. And it always takes present -는 둥; 먹은 둥 마는 둥 is wrong for this 'half-heartedly' meaning.
usage: 밥을 먹는 둥 마는 둥 했어요
I barely picked at my food
Ate without appetite — describes the sloppy manner, then capped with 했어요
대답을 하는 둥 마는 둥 하더라고요
He answered half-heartedly, I noticed
Distracted reply + -더라고요 (reporting what you witnessed)
공부를 하는 둥 마는 둥 해
He studies half-heartedly
Not really focused; present -는 둥 throughout
듣는 둥 마는 둥 하지 마
Don't half-listen to me
Casual complaint; 마는 둥 (ㄹ dropped), never 말는 둥
examples: 아침에 늦어서 밥을 먹는 둥 마는 둥 하고 뛰어나왔어요.
I was late, so I barely touched my breakfast and ran out.
Hurried morning; -고 links the half-eaten meal to dashing out
걔는 내 말을 듣는 둥 마는 둥 하고 계속 폰만 봤어.
He half-listened to me and just kept staring at his phone.
폰만 보다 = glued to phone; the pattern conveys mild annoyance at the inattention
주말 내내 일하는 둥 마는 둥 하면서 넷플릭스만 봤어요.
All weekend I sort of worked but mostly just watched Netflix.
내내 = the whole time; -면서 shows the half-work happening alongside Netflix
mistakes: Writing 말는 둥 — the present modifier of 말다 is 마는 (ㄹ drops before -는), so it's 마는 둥.
Using a past modifier (먹은 둥 마는 둥) for the half-hearted meaning — this pattern is fixed with present -는 둥.
Confusing it with -(으)나 마나. 먹는 둥 마는 둥 = 'ate it half-heartedly (manner)'; 먹으나 마나 = 'no point eating (futile result).'

english: also for the purpose of / partly to (doing two things at once)
formNote: 겸 is the Sino-Korean dependent noun 兼 ('combine, hold concurrently'), so -(으)ㄹ 겸 frames one action as serving two aims at once — 'partly in order to ~ (and partly for something else).' Attach -ㄹ 겸 to vowel stems (보다 → 볼 겸), -을 겸 to consonant stems (먹다 → 먹을 겸); ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ (놀다 → 놀 겸). It very often comes doubled: A-(으)ㄹ 겸 B-(으)ㄹ 겸 ('partly to A, partly to B'), and a main action follows. CONTRAST: -(으)ㄹ 겸 vs -(으)러 (purpose 'in order to') — -(으)러 names the single main reason for going/coming (밥 먹으러 가다 = 'go in order to eat'), while -(으)ㄹ 겸 adds a SECONDARY purpose riding along ('while I'm at it, also to ~'), implying there's already another reason. So 산책할 겸 나왔어요 = 'I came out, and a walk was one of the reasons too.' REGISTER: neutral, everyday; great for casually justifying outings and two-birds-one-stone plans. PITFALL #1: use the future modifier -(으)ㄹ, never -는 겸 (볼 겸, not 보는 겸). PITFALL #2: 겸 cannot end a sentence by itself like a finite verb — it needs a following main action (볼 겸 왔어요), so don't stop at 볼 겸이에요.
usage: 바람도 쐴 겸 산책해요
I take a walk partly to get some air
쐬다 → 쐴 겸; the 도 ('also') signals this is one of several reasons
운동도 할 겸 걸어가요
I walk there, also to get some exercise
Two-in-one rationale; the walking serves the exercise aim on the side
친구도 볼 겸 서울 가요
I'm going to Seoul, partly to see a friend
Combining errands; seeing the friend is a secondary purpose
밥도 먹을 겸 만나자
Let's meet, and grab a meal while we're at it
겸 + suggestion -자; eating is the bonus purpose of meeting
examples: 바람도 쐴 겸 머리도 식힐 겸 한강에 나왔어요.
I came out to the Han River partly for fresh air, partly to clear my head.
Doubled 겸...겸 listing two aims; 머리(를) 식히다 = clear one's head
맛집 탐방도 할 겸 데이트 겸 해서 성수동 갔어요.
We went to Seongsu-dong both to hit good restaurants and for a date.
성수동 = trendy Seoul area; 탐방 = exploring; N 겸 해서 bundles a noun-purpose too
운동도 할 겸 출근은 자전거로 해요.
I commute by bike, partly to get some exercise.
출근 = commute to work; the bike commute doubles as a workout
mistakes: Using the present modifier 보는 겸 — it's the future modifier -(으)ㄹ + 겸 (볼 겸).
Ending the sentence on 겸 (볼 겸이에요) — 겸 demands a following main action, e.g. 볼 겸 왔어요.
Substituting -(으)러 when there are two reasons. -(으)러 gives the single main purpose (보러 가다); -(으)ㄹ 겸 adds a side purpose to an action you'd do anyway.

english: tends to be / is on the ... side (rather than strongly)
formNote: 편 is the Sino-Korean noun 便 ('side, group, leaning'), so '-(으)ㄴ/는 편이다' literally places something 'on the ~ side,' softening a claim from 'very' to 'rather/relatively.' Verbs take -는 편이다 (먹다 → 먹는 편이다), adjectives -(으)ㄴ 편이다 (크다 → 큰 편이다, 작다 → 작은 편이다); past habits use -(으)ㄴ 편이었다. CONTRAST: -(으)ㄴ/는 편이다 vs the bare adjective — 키가 커요 asserts 'I am tall' flatly, while 키가 큰 편이에요 hedges to 'I'm on the taller side,' relative to others, sounding modest and non-absolute. It also differs from -(으)ㄴ/는 척하다 ('pretend to be') despite both using a 편/척 + 이다/하다 frame — 편이다 is an honest mild judgment, not a pretense. REGISTER: neutral and very polite-friendly; Koreans use it constantly for self-description and comparisons to avoid sounding boastful or blunt (술은 약한 편이에요 is gentler than 술 못 마셔요). PITFALL #1: match the modifier to word type — verbs -는 편 (먹는 편), adjectives -(으)ㄴ 편 (큰 편), so never 크는 편. PITFALL #2: because it means 'relatively,' don't pair it with intensifiers like 아주/완전 ('totally'); that contradicts the very softening it provides.
usage: 저는 매운 거 잘 먹는 편이에요
I'm on the side of handling spicy food well
Verb 먹다 → -는 편; hedges a habit modestly
키가 큰 편이에요
I'm fairly tall
Adjective 크다 → -(으)ㄴ 편; 'taller side,' not flatly 'tall'
술은 약한 편이야
I'm a bit of a lightweight with alcohol
약하다 → 약한 편; gentler than 술 못 마셔
월급은 적은 편이에요
My salary is on the lower side
Modest, hedged self-description of a sensitive topic
examples: 저는 집순이라서 주말엔 집에 있는 편이에요.
I'm a homebody, so I tend to stay in on weekends.
집순이 = stay-at-home type; verb 있다 → 있는 편 for a tendency
여긴 다른 동네보다 월세가 싼 편이라 들어왔어요.
Rent here is on the cheaper side than other areas, so I moved in.
Comparison with 보다 ('than'); 싼 편이라 = 'being on the cheaper side, so...'
저는 낯을 좀 가리는 편이라 회식이 부담돼요.
I'm rather shy with new people, so company dinners stress me out.
낯을 가리다 = be shy with strangers; 부담되다 = feel pressured; 좀 doubles the hedge
mistakes: Mismatching the modifier: verbs take -는 편 (먹는 편), adjectives take -(으)ㄴ 편 (큰 편) — don't say 크는 편.
Pairing it with 아주/완전 ('totally, completely') — it means 'relatively,' so intensifiers clash with the softening; say 키가 큰 편이에요, not 아주 큰 편이에요.
Using it when you mean an absolute fact. If something is definitely true, state it plainly; 편이다 specifically signals 'comparatively, on the ~ side.'

english: do (it), but... / it's true that ~, though (conceding then qualifying)
formNote: Built from the nominalizer -기 + the contrast topic particle 는 + a dummy 하다 that echoes the verb's meaning, so it isolates and concedes one point ('as for doing it, yes') while signaling a 'but' is coming. Attach -기는 하다 to a verb or adjective stem (먹다 → 먹기는 하다, 좋다 → 좋기는 하다); in speech 기는 almost always contracts to 긴 (먹긴 해요). For tense, conjugate the final 하다 (먹기는 했어요 = 'I did eat, but...'); you can also fully repeat the verb instead of using 하다 (가긴 가다, 좋긴 좋다). CONTRAST: -기는 하다 vs -지만 — both pivot to a contrast, but -지만 is a neutral 'but' joining two clauses (좋지만 비싸요 = 'it's good but expensive'), whereas -기는 하다 first GRANTS/concedes the point with extra emphasis ('it IS good, I'll give you that... but'), carrying a reluctant, qualifying tone. So 좋긴 한데 비싸요 admits the merit before pushing back. It's usually followed by 그런데/근데 or -지만/-(으)ㄴ데. REGISTER: conversational and very common for soft disagreement, polite hedging, or a gentle 'no.' PITFALL: don't drop the verb's meaning into a bare 하다 — 가긴 하다 keeps 'go' via the repeated stem (or you say 가긴 가다); 가는 하다 is wrong. And since it sets up a contrast, 좋긴 해요 left alone feels unfinished unless the 'but' is understood.
usage: 먹기는 했어요
I did eat it (but...)
Conceding before a 'but'; tense lives on the final 하다 → 했어요
좋긴 한데 비싸요
It's good, but it's pricey
긴 contraction + -(으)ㄴ데; grants the merit, then qualifies
가긴 갈 건데 늦을 거야
I'll go, but I'll be late
Full repetition 가긴 가다 instead of 하다; -(으)ㄹ 건데 looks ahead
알긴 아는데 설명을 못 하겠어요
I do know it, but I can't explain it
알다 → 알긴 알다 (repeated stem); concession + limitation
examples: 그 사람 착하긴 한데 좀 제 스타일은 아니에요.
He is nice, but he's just not my type.
Dating soft no; 착하다 = kind; 한데 pivots to the gentle rejection
회사 다니긴 다니는데 요즘 이직 생각 중이에요.
I am working at the company, but I'm thinking of switching jobs lately.
이직 = job change; full repeat 다니긴 다니다 then -는데 turns to the 'but'
맵긴 매운데 진짜 맛있어서 계속 손이 가요.
It is spicy, but it's so good I can't stop reaching for it.
손이 가다 = keep reaching for; 맵긴 맵다 concedes the spice before the upside
mistakes: Collapsing the verb into a bare 하다 (가는 하다) — you must repeat the action's meaning: 가긴 하다, or fully 가긴 가다.
Leaving it hanging without the contrast. It exists to set up a 'but,' so 좋긴 해요 by itself feels incomplete unless the qualifier is clearly implied.
Reaching for plain -지만 when you want to first concede with emphasis. -지만 is a neutral 'but'; -기는 하다 grants the point ('it IS good, granted...') before pushing back.
